The core mechanism of joint-feeling projection operates through a dual-process model: first, a local sensory signal (J) is encoded in neural space; second, this signal is projected via a cognitive kernel K(S) to a target spatial region. The here-there duality emerges as a topological constraint, where H represents the observer’s internal reference frame and T denotes the external target. The intervening space I mediates this transition, requiring conscious awareness C(I) to maintain fidelity. When I shrinks to zero, the system collapses to a point-sensor model; when I expands, symbolic abstraction dominates. This framework supports both direct perception (within body) and indirect projection (beyond body), with failure modes occurring at boundary conditions where C(I) drops below critical thresholds. The system exhibits a phase transition from localized to distributed spatial representation as I increases.
